title: Event Triggered Execution: Accessibility Features
summary: The Windows logon screen starts accessibility helpers such as sethc.exe, the Sticky Keys program, and utilman.exe, the Utility Manager, inside the winlogon session before any user has authenticated. An adversary abuses the keyboard shortcut that starts those helpers, either by overwriting the helper binary in the system folder or by repointing the registry references that name it, so the shortcut launches attacker code instead. Because the trigger fires on the secure desktop, that code executes as SYSTEM without a valid logon. The artefacts are a changed hash or broken signature on an accessibility binary, new files placed beside it, writes under the Accessibility and Image File Execution Options registry paths, and process creation where a signed accessibility image is the parent of a command shell. The reliable discriminator is the parent-child chain, because genuine helpers are Microsoft-signed and never start a shell.

beginner.definition: This technique makes a computer run an attacker's program at the logon screen. On Windows, pressing Shift five times or the Windows key with U starts small helper tools. These tools help people who have trouble seeing, hearing or typing. An attacker replaces one helper tool with their own program. The helper, and the attacker's code, then run before anyone signs in.
beginner.whyItMatters: The logon screen is trusted, so code that runs there may run as SYSTEM, a built-in account with very high rights. The same shortcut also works over a remote desktop session, so an attacker may not need to sit at the machine. A change of this kind usually survives a restart, and it can be easy to miss. If you ignore it, an intruder can return to a signed-out computer again and again.
howItWorks: Windows offers accessibility helpers such as Sticky Keys, and a set key combination starts each one.
An attacker who already holds administrator rights copies their own program over the helper file in the system folder.
Another method edits a registry value that tells Windows which file the key combination should start.
At the next logon screen, the shortcut starts the attacker's file instead of the real helper.
The program runs on the secure desktop as SYSTEM, so it needs no password at all.
On newer Windows versions a replaced file must be digitally signed, so attackers move to registry methods.
beginner.example: Picture a hospital night desk with a red button marked call the nurse. The button exists for patients who cannot reach the telephone. Someone swaps the label behind the button, so it now calls a stranger outside the building. Staff still trust the button, because it sits in the same place and looks the same. Nobody checks who answers until the damage is done. Accessibility shortcuts work in the same way. The key combination is the button, the helper program is the label, and the attacker quietly changes the label.
takeaways: Accessibility shortcuts can start code as SYSTEM, so treat the logon screen as a sensitive place.
Check the digital signature and file hash of Sticky Keys and Utility Manager, not only the file name.
Raise an alert when a signed accessibility program starts a command shell.

objectives: Explain what an accessibility feature is and why it can run before logon.
Describe how binary replacement and registry redirection both abuse accessibility shortcuts.
Identify the log sources that record file changes and process creation at the logon screen.
Distinguish a genuine accessibility helper from a replaced one using signatures and parent processes.
List the accessibility programs an attacker is most likely to target.
Recommend one control that reduces the value of this technique.
